request_echo: 58F, resistant hypertension despite ACEi + CCB + thiazide at max dose; elevated hs-CRP; poor response to RAAS blockade.

axes.rationale: Explicit poor response to RAAS blockade despite ACEi at maximum dose indicates potential RAAS pathway dysfunction or inadequate suppression; suggests need to evaluate aldosterone breakthrough, renin escape, or alternative RAAS mechanisms

Elevated hs-CRP indicates systemic inflammation as a potential driver of resistant hypertension; inflammatory pathways may contribute to endothelial dysfunction and vascular stiffness independent of RAAS

Resistant hypertension with elevated inflammatory markers suggests endothelial dysfunction and vascular stiffness as underlying mechanisms; poor RAAS response may reflect structural/functional vascular pathology
Thiazide diuretic at max dose with persistent hypertension raises concern for volume-resistant hypertension; may indicate renal sodium retention mechanisms or primary renal pathology
Poor response to standard triple therapy (ACEi/CCB/thiazide) despite maximum dosing suggests possible pharmacogenomic factors affecting drug metabolism or target responsiveness

hypothesis.statement: Aldosterone breakthrough via non-ACE-dependent chymase-mediated angiotensin II generation in renal tubular cells drives persistent mineralocorticoid receptor activation, causing thiazide-refractory sodium retention independent of ACE inhibition. This mechanism is amplified in post-menopausal women (reduced estrogen-mediated suppression of chymase expression) and in individuals with CKD-associated tubular hypertrophy.
hypothesis.prediction: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio will remain elevated (>30 ng/dL per ng/mL/hr) despite maximum ACEi dosing; urinary aldosterone excretion will not fall proportionally to plasma ACE activity; renal biopsy or urinary chymase activity assay will show elevated chymase in tubular epithelium; adding a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone) will reduce 24-hour urinary sodium excretion by >40 mEq/day and lower systolic BP >15 mmHg, whereas continuing ACEi dose escalation will not.
hypothesis.rationale: ACE inhibitors block only one of at least two enzymatic routes to angiotensin II; mast-cell and tubular chymase can generate Ang II independently. Post-menopausal estrogen loss removes a known suppressor of chymase transcription. Elevated hs-CRP suggests mast-cell degranulation and inflammatory microenvironment in the kidney, which would further upregulate chymase. This is a genuinely open mechanistic question because chymase contribution to human renal Ang II generation in vivo is not quantified in clinical practice, and the interaction with menopausal status is uncharacterized at the pathway level.

evidence.claim_fragment: To show that the frequency of aldosterone breakthrough is lower when RAS blockers are given at bedtime compared to on awaking, and to analyze the determinants and consequences of aldosterone breakthrough.

reference.title: RAS Blockade at Bedtime Versus on Awakening for Aldosterone Breakthrough

hypotheses.novelty_reason: The core phenomenon of aldosterone breakthrough via chymase-mediated angiotensin II generation despite ACE inhibition is documented in the literature (chymase as an ACE-independent pathway is established; aldosterone breakthrough under ACEi is established). However, the specific mechanistic localization to renal tubular cells as the primary driver of thiazide-refractory sodium retention, combined with the sex-specific amplification via estrogen-mediated chymase suppression in post-menopausal women and the CKD-tubular hypertrophy amplification, represents a more granular and incompletely tested synthesis. The provided RCT evidence is tangentially relevant (aldosterone breakthrough timing with RAS blockers) but does not directly test the tubular chymase mechanism, the post-menopausal modifier, or the CKD-hypertrophy interaction. The specific predictions (urinary chymase assay, differential response to MRA vs. ACEi escalation in these subgroups) are not well-documented. This makes the hypothesis plausible and partially supported by mechanistic literature but unresolved as a unified clinical entity, qualifying it as a good investigative target rather than either established or wholly unsupported.

hypothesis.statement: Clonally expanded CD8+ effector-memory T cells infiltrating the perivascular adventitia produce IFN-γ and IL-17A, which transcriptionally suppress endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) via STAT1-mediated promoter methylation and simultaneously upregulate NADPH oxidase (NOX2) in vascular smooth muscle, creating a self-sustaining oxidative-inflammatory loop that maintains elevated vascular resistance independently of RAAS activity.
hypothesis.prediction: Peripheral blood immunophenotyping will show an elevated CD8+ effector-memory (CD45RA−CCR7−) to naïve T-cell ratio compared to age-sex-matched normotensive controls; plasma IFN-γ and IL-17A will be elevated; ex vivo stimulation of patient PBMCs will produce greater IFN-γ secretion per cell than controls; aortic pulse-wave velocity (a surrogate for vascular stiffness) will correlate positively with CD8+ effector-memory cell count (r > 0.5 in a cohort study); methylation-specific PCR of circulating endothelial cells will show hypermethylation of the eNOS promoter CpG island relative to normotensive controls; and selective depletion or blockade of IFN-γ signaling in a humanized mouse model of this phenotype will reduce vascular NOX2 expression and restore NO bioavailability.
hypothesis.rationale: Elevated hs-CRP in resistant hypertension is often attributed generically to inflammation, but the specific effector arm is rarely specified. CD8+ T-cell-mediated vascular inflammation has been demonstrated in animal models of Ang II-induced hypertension, yet the human in vivo evidence for eNOS promoter methylation downstream of IFN-γ/STAT1 as a durable, drug-resistant mechanism is an open question. This would explain why RAAS blockade and CCB fail: the primary lesion is transcriptional suppression of vasodilatory capacity, not excess vasoconstrictor signaling. Population modifier: post-menopausal women have higher Th1/Th17 skewing relative to pre-menopausal women, potentially amplifying this axis.

hypotheses.novelty_reason: The hypothesis integrates several individually plausible but incompletely connected mechanisms. CD8+ T-cell involvement in hypertension and vascular inflammation has partial experimental support (Guzik et al., Madhur et al.), and IFN-γ/IL-17A roles in vascular dysfunction are documented. However, the specific mechanistic chain—clonally expanded CD8+ effector-memory cells in the perivascular adventitia → STAT1-mediated eNOS promoter methylation (epigenetic suppression specifically) → simultaneous NOX2 upregulation in VSMC → RAAS-independent self-sustaining loop—has not been established as a unified, validated pathway. The eNOS epigenetic suppression via STAT1-driven methylation specifically downstream of T-cell-derived cytokines is not well-documented, nor is the RAAS-independence claim rigorously tested. The predictions are experimentally tractable and the hypothesis is mechanistically coherent, making it a genuine open question rather than either established dogma or unsupported speculation.

hypothesis.statement: A loss-of-function variant in SLC12A3 (encoding the thiazide-sensitive NCC cotransporter) paradoxically causes compensatory upregulation of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) via aldosterone-independent WNK1/SPAK kinase pathway activation, such that thiazide occupancy of NCC triggers a homeostatic rebound that fully restores sodium reabsorption through ENaC, rendering the diuretic component of triple therapy ineffective and maintaining volume-dependent hypertension.
hypothesis.prediction: Whole-exome sequencing will identify a heterozygous hypomorphic SLC12A3 variant (minor allele frequency <2%) in this patient; urinary sodium excretion will not increase acutely (within 6 hours) after a supervised thiazide dose challenge compared to wild-type controls; urinary ENaC activity (estimated by lithium clearance ratio or amiloride-sensitive natriuresis) will be disproportionately elevated relative to plasma aldosterone; phospho-SPAK levels in urinary exosomes will be elevated at baseline; and adding amiloride (ENaC blocker) will produce a natriuretic response exceeding that of continued thiazide, with a predicted systolic BP reduction >12 mmHg that is not seen with thiazide dose escalation.
hypothesis.rationale: SLC12A3 variants are known to cause Gitelman syndrome at homozygous loss-of-function, but heterozygous hypomorphic states create a nuanced phenotype where partial NCC dysfunction activates WNK-SPAK signaling as a compensatory mechanism, potentially upregulating ENaC beyond baseline. This is an open mechanistic question because the net blood pressure effect of heterozygous SLC12A3 variants in the context of triple antihypertensive therapy has not been characterized, and the WNK1/SPAK-ENaC compensatory axis in humans under pharmacological NCC blockade is not well-defined. This would explain thiazide refractoriness without invoking non-adherence or secondary causes, and is testable with urinary exosome phosphoproteomics—a currently feasible but underutilized clinical research tool.

evidence.claim_fragment: Gitelman syndrome is recessively inherited, caused by inactivating mutations in the SLC12A3 gene that encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC)

reference.title: Gitelman syndrome: consensus and guidance from a Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Controversies Conference.

evidence.claim_fragment: The thiazide-sensitive Na(+)-Cl(-) cotransporter (TSC) is responsible for the major sodium chloride reabsorption pathway; TSC mutants are associated with Gitelman's syndrome and human hypertension

reference.title: Thiazide-sensitive Na+-Cl- cotransporter: genetic polymorphisms and human diseases.

hypotheses.novelty_reason: The core components are individually established: SLC12A3 loss-of-function causes Gitelman syndrome (supported), WNK1/SPAK signaling regulates NCC and ENaC (well-documented in renal physiology literature), and compensatory ENaC upregulation in NCC-deficient states has been observed in animal models. However, the specific mechanistic claim—that heterozygous hypomorphic SLC12A3 variants drive aldosterone-independent WNK1/SPAK-mediated ENaC upregulation sufficient to fully nullify thiazide diuretic efficacy in a hypertensive patient, and that this constitutes a clinically actionable pharmacogenomic resistance mechanism detectable via urinary exosome phospho-SPAK—is not established in the literature. The aldosterone-independent framing of ENaC compensation in this context, the predicted complete blunting of thiazide natriuresis in heterozygotes (rather than full Gitelman homozygotes), and the specific therapeutic prediction (amiloride superiority >12 mmHg SBP reduction) represent a plausible but unresolved synthesis that goes beyond current evidence. The hypothesis is mechanistically coherent and partially grounded but lacks direct human clinical validation, making it a legitimate open question rather than either established or unsupported. (citing PMID 28003083, PMID 25841442)

top_experiment.question: Do kidney distal tubule cells in Tabula Sapiens show co-expression of SLC12A3 (NCC), WNK1/SPAK pathway genes (WNK1, WNK4, STK39/SPAK, OXSR1), and ENaC subunits (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G) in a pattern consistent with a compensatory WNK-SPAK→ENaC axis that could sustain sodium reabsorption when NCC is functionally reduced?
top_experiment.method: Single-cell transcriptomic co-expression and gene-module analysis of kidney distal tubule cells from Tabula Sapiens to test whether the WNK1/SPAK signaling axis and ENaC subunit genes are transcriptionally coupled to SLC12A3 expression levels, and whether cells with low SLC12A3 expression show compensatory upregulation of WNK1/SPAK pathway and ENaC genes — a transcriptional proxy for the proposed compensatory mechanism.
protocol_steps: 1. Download the Tabula Sapiens kidney compartment h5ad file from the portal (TabulaSapiens.h5ad or the organ-specific kidney subset); load into scanpy (Python) or Seurat (R).

2. Subset to kidney cells only (obs['organ_tissue'] == 'Kidney'); inspect cell-type annotations to identify distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and connecting tubule (CNT) clusters — expected labels include 'distal convoluted tubule epithelial cell', 'connecting tubule cell', or equivalent UBERON/CL ontology terms.

3. Define the gene panel of interest: NCC_gene = 'SLC12A3'; WNK_SPAK_genes = ['WNK1','WNK4','STK39','OXSR1','CLDN7','CLDN10']; ENaC_genes = ['SCNN1A','SCNN1B','SCNN1G']; aldosterone_sensor = ['NR3C2']; control_housekeeping = ['ACTB','GAPDH'].
4. Within DCT/CNT cells, compute per-cell normalized log-expression (scanpy: sc.pp.normalize_total + sc.pp.log1p if not already normalized) for all genes in the panel.

5. Stratify DCT/CNT cells into SLC12A3-low (bottom tertile of expression) vs SLC12A3-high (top tertile) groups. Perform Wilcoxon rank-sum tests comparing WNK_SPAK_genes and ENaC_genes expression between the two groups; apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.
6. Compute pairwise Spearman correlation coefficients among all panel genes within DCT/CNT cells; visualize as a clustered heatmap to reveal co-expression modules.

7. Score each DCT/CNT cell for a 'WNK_SPAK_ENaC_module' using scanpy sc.tl.score_genes() with WNK_SPAK_genes + ENaC_genes as the gene set; plot module score as a function of SLC12A3 expression (scatter + LOWESS fit) and test for a significant negative correlation (Spearman rho < 0, p < 0.05).

8. Separately score a 'NR3C2_aldosterone_module' (NR3C2 + known aldosterone-responsive genes: SCNN1B, FKBP5, SGK1) and test whether the WNK_SPAK_ENaC module score is elevated in SLC12A3-low cells independently of NR3C2 module score, using partial correlation or linear regression controlling for NR3C2 expression.

9. Extend analysis to other kidney cell types (proximal tubule, thick ascending limb, collecting duct principal cells) as negative/positive controls: ENaC genes should be highest in collecting duct; SLC12A3 should be DCT-specific.
10. Generate a UMAP of all kidney cells colored by SLC12A3, WNK1, STK39, SCNN1B expression and by WNK_SPAK_ENaC module score; export figures as PDF/PNG for reporting.
top_experiment.confirm_if: In DCT/CNT cells, SLC12A3-low cells show statistically significant upregulation of ≥2 WNK_SPAK pathway genes (WNK1, WNK4, STK39, or OXSR1) AND ≥1 ENaC subunit gene (SCNN1A/B/G) compared to SLC12A3-high cells (FDR < 0.10); AND the WNK_SPAK_ENaC module score is negatively correlated with SLC12A3 expression (Spearman rho < −0.15, p < 0.05); AND this association persists after controlling for NR3C2 expression, supporting an aldosterone-independent compensatory axis.
top_experiment.refute_if: SLC12A3-low DCT/CNT cells show no significant upregulation of WNK_SPAK or ENaC genes (all FDR > 0.10); OR the WNK_SPAK_ENaC module score is positively correlated with SLC12A3 (rho > 0), indicating co-expression rather than compensation; OR any apparent ENaC upregulation is fully explained by NR3C2/aldosterone-pathway co-expression, negating the aldosterone-independent WNK-SPAK mechanism proposed in the hypothesis.
top_experiment.feasibility_notes: Tabula Sapiens is used here as the pinned default substrate per BUILD_SPEC.md §8 because the previously proposed GEO accession was rejected. The kidney compartment of Tabula Sapiens (v1.0, ~11 donors, ~30,000 kidney cells) does contain annotated DCT and CNT cell populations with sufficient coverage for this analysis. SLC12A3 is a marker gene for DCT cells in this atlas and is expected to be detectable. WNK1, STK39, and SCNN1B have been reported as expressed in human kidney single-cell data. Caveat: single-cell RNA-seq captures transcriptional state, not post-translational phosphorylation (phospho-SPAK), so this experiment tests the transcriptional plausibility of the compensatory axis rather than its functional activation. Cell numbers in DCT/CNT clusters may be modest (~200–800 cells across donors), which limits statistical power; tertile stratification within a single cell type may yield small groups. The analysis is fully executable in Python/scanpy with the public h5ad download and requires no additional data beyond Tabula Sapiens. Fell back to the pinned default substrate (Tabula Sapiens immune compartment) because the proposed dataset could not be verified to actually BE the dataset it claimed to be (BUILD_SPEC.md §5: never emit a fabricated/guessed accession; Phase 5/7 verify dataset_pointer actually resolves to a matching dataset, not merely to *a* record). (Original proposal rejected: claimed dataset content does not match the real GEO record (real title: 'Single Cell Transcriptional Analysis of Donor and Recipient Immune Cell Chimerism in the Rejecting Kidney Transplant'; shared keywords: ['kidney', 'rna-seq', 'variation', 'whole-exome']).)
top_experiment.claude_science_prompt:
Using the Tabula Sapiens kidney compartment single-cell RNA-seq data (download from https://tabula-sapiens-portal.ds.czbiohub.org/, kidney organ h5ad), please perform the following analysis and produce a multi-panel figure:

1. Load the kidney h5ad into scanpy. Subset to distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and connecting tubule (CNT) cells based on cell_type annotation.

2. For the gene panel [SLC12A3, WNK1, WNK4, STK39, OXSR1, SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G, NR3C2, SGK1, FKBP5], extract normalized log-expression values per cell.

3. Stratify DCT/CNT cells into SLC12A3-low (bottom tertile) vs SLC12A3-high (top tertile). Run Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for each gene comparing the two groups; apply BH FDR correction. Report a table of log2 fold-changes and FDR values.

4. Compute a Spearman correlation matrix among all panel genes within DCT/CNT cells and plot as a clustered heatmap (Panel A).

5. Score each DCT/CNT cell for a WNK_SPAK_ENaC module (genes: WNK1, WNK4, STK39, OXSR1, SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G) using sc.tl.score_genes(). Plot module score vs SLC12A3 expression as a scatter plot with LOWESS fit and Spearman rho annotation (Panel B).

6. Run a linear regression of WNK_SPAK_ENaC module score ~ SLC12A3_expression + NR3C2_expression within DCT/CNT cells. Report coefficients and p-values to test aldosterone-independence (Panel C: partial regression plot for SLC12A3 coefficient).

7. Generate a UMAP of all kidney cells colored by SLC12A3 and SCNN1B expression (Panel D).

8. Produce a violin plot comparing WNK1, STK39, and SCNN1B expression between SLC12A3-low and SLC12A3-high DCT/CNT cells with FDR-corrected significance bars (Panel E).

Output: a 5-panel PDF figure with a summary statistics table. State clearly whether results confirm or refute the hypothesis that SLC12A3-low DCT cells show aldosterone-independent upregulation of the WNK-SPAK-ENaC axis.

uncertainty_note: All three hypotheses represent plausible but incompletely validated mechanistic syntheses. H1 and H2 lack direct experimental evidence for their proposed unified pathways—specifically, the tubular chymase-driven sodium retention amplified by post-menopausal status (H1) and the STAT1-mediated eNOS epigenetic suppression downstream of clonal CD8+ T cells (H2) remain unproven despite individually supported components. H3 is better grounded in established renal physiology but the specific claim that heterozygous SLC12A3 variants cause complete thiazide resistance through aldosterone-independent ENaC compensation has not been clinically validated. Readers should recognize that while these mechanisms are mechanistically coherent and address genuine clinical gaps (thiazide-refractory hypertension, sex-specific responses, pharmacogenomic resistance), the evidence linking component mechanisms into unified causal chains remains thin, and the predicted clinical consequences and biomarkers (urinary chymase, phospho-SPAK, differential MRA response) are largely untested.

abstracts.abstract:
Objective:

To show that the frequency of aldosterone breakthrough is lower when RAS blockers are given at bedtime compared to on awaking, and to analyze the determinants and consequences of aldosterone breakthrough.

Duration of the study: Inclusion 2 years, follow-up one year, total 3 years Design: prospective, multicenter, randomized, controlled, open label, two parallel groups.

Main selection criteria:

Inclusion criteria

* Chronic kidney disease stage 3 to 4,
* ACEI (captopril, enalapril, or ramipril), and/or ARB (losartan, valsartan, or irbesartan) on awaking for at least three months,
interventions: Randomization that determine the time of treatment

abstracts.title: Eplerenone for Subclinical Cardiomyopathy in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
abstracts.abstract:
Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), the most common muscular dystrophy, leads to skeletal and cardiac muscle damage. Treatment of pulmonary complications has improved survival; however, heart muscle disease or cardiomyopathy has emerged as a leading cause of death, typically by the third decade. Although myocardial changes begin early, clinically significant heart disease is rarely detected in the first decade of life. Consequently, DMD cardiomyopathy frequently goes unrecognized (and untreated) until advanced (and irreversible).

Current DMD cardiovascular care guidelines recommend beta-blocke

abstracts.title: Polymorphisms within Autophagy-Related Genes as Susceptibility Biomarkers for Multiple Myeloma: A Meta-Analysis of Three Large Cohorts and Functional Characterization.
abstracts.abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) arises following malignant proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow, that secrete high amounts of specific monoclonal immunoglobulins or light chains, resulting in the massive production of unfolded or misfolded proteins. Autophagy can have a dual role in tumorigenesis, by eliminating these abnormal proteins to avoid cancer development, but also ensuring MM cell survival and promoting resistance to treatments. To date no studies have determined the impact of genetic variation in autophagy-related genes on MM risk. We performed meta-analysis of germline genetic data on 234 autophagy-related genes from three independent study populations including 13,387 subjects of European ancestry (6863 MM patients and 6524 controls) and examined correlations of statistically significant single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs; p < 1 × 10-9) with immune responses in whole blood, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDM) from a large population of healthy donors from the Human Functional Genomic Project (HFGP). We identified SNPs in six loci, CD46, IKBKE, PARK2, ULK4, ATG5, and CDKN2A associated with MM risk (p = 4.47 × 10-4-5.79 × 10-14). Mechanistically, we found that the ULK4rs6599175 SNP correlated with circulating concentrations of vitamin D3 (p = 4.0 × 10-4), whereas the IKBKErs17433804 SNP correlated with the number of transitional CD24+CD38+ B cells (p = 4.8 × 10-4) and circulating serum concentrations of Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein (MCP)-2 (p = 3.6 × 10-4). We also found that the CD46rs1142469 SNP correlated with numbers of CD19+ B cells, CD19+CD3- B cells, CD5+IgD- cells, IgM- cells, IgD-IgM- cells, and CD4-CD8- PBMCs (p = 4.9 × 10-4-8.6 × 10-4) and circulating concentrations of interleukin (IL)-20 (p = 0.00082). Finally, we observed that the CDKN2Ars2811710 SNP correlated with levels of CD4+EMCD45RO+CD27- cells (p = 9.3 × 10-4). These results suggest that genetic variants within these six loci influence MM risk through the modulation of specific subsets of immune cells, as well as vitamin D3-, MCP-2-, and IL20-dependent pathways.
abstracts.full_text: Simple SummaryWe investigated the influence of autophagy-related variants in modulating Multiple Myeloma (MM) risk through a meta-analysis of germline genetic data on 234 autophagy-related genes from three independent study populations including 13,387 subjects of European ancestry (6863 MM patients and 6524 controls) and examined the functional mechanisms behind the observed associations. We identified SNPs within the six CD46, IKBKE, PARK2, ULK4, ATG5, and CDKN2A loci associated with MM risk and observed that their effect on disease risk was mediated by specific subsets of immune cells, as well as vitamin D3-, MCP-2-, and IL20-dependent mechanisms.AbstractMultiple myeloma (MM) arises following malignant proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow, that secrete high amounts of specific monoclonal immunoglobulins or light chains, resulting in the massive production of unfolded or misfolded proteins. Autophagy can have a dual role in tumorigenesis, by eliminating these abnormal proteins to avoid cancer development, but also ensuring MM cell survival and promoting resistance to treatments. To date no studies have determined the impact of genetic variation in autophagy-related genes on MM risk. We performed meta-analysis of germline genetic data on 234 autophagy-related genes from three independent study populations including 13,387 subjects of European ancestry (6863 MM patients and 6524 controls) and examined correlations of statistically significant single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs; p < 1 × 10−9) with immune responses in whole blood, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDM) from a large population of healthy donors from the Human Functional Genomic Project (HFGP). We identified SNPs in six loci, CD46, IKBKE, PARK2, ULK4, ATG5, and CDKN2A associated with MM risk (p = 4.47 × 10−4−5.79 × 10−14). Mechanistically, we found that the ULK4rs6599175 SNP correlated with circulating concentrations of vitamin D3 (p = 4.0 × 10−4), whereas the IKBKErs17433804 SNP correlated with the number of transitional CD24+CD38+ B cells (p = 4.8 × 10−4) and circulating serum concentrations of Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein (MCP)-2 (p = 3.6 × 10−4). We also found that the CD46rs1142469 SNP correlated with numbers of CD19+ B cells, CD19+CD3− B cells, CD5+IgD− cells, IgM− cells, IgD−IgM− cells, and CD4−CD8− PBMCs (p = 4.9 × 10−4−8.6 × 10−4) and circulating concentrations of interleukin (IL)-20 (p = 0.00082). Finally, we observed that the CDKN2Ars2811710 SNP correlated with levels of CD4+EMCD45RO+CD27− cells (p = 9.3 × 10−4). These results suggest that genetic variants within these six loci influence MM risk through the modulation of specific subsets of immune cells, as well as vitamin D3−, MCP-2−, and IL20-dependent pathways. 1. IntroductionMultiple myeloma (MM) is a relatively common and incurable hematological malignancy arising from post–germinal mature B cells and it is characterized by the presence of proliferating plasma cells in the bone marrow that secrete specific monoclonal immunoglobulin (also called M-protein) [1]. Given the exacerbated production of immunoglobulin, MM patients often suffer from a concomitant decrease in normal immunoglobulins [2] that causes immune dysfunction, increases susceptibility to opportunistic infections, and impacts on disease severity and prognosis [3,4].Although the high production of monoclonal immunoglobulins occurring in MM invariably results in the presence of a high amount of unfolded or misfolded proteins that might be toxic for MM cells in the bone marrow, recent studies demonstrated that plasma cells are able to exploit molecular pathways to protect themselves from damage caused by toxic proteins [5]. These molecular pathways include the activation of unfolded protein response (UPR) [6,7,8], heat protein chaperones [9], aggresome formation [10], and the induction of cellular autophagy [5]. Autophagy is a lysosome-dependent catabolic degradation process by which cells remove toxic aggregated cytosolic proteins and malfunctioning organelles. It has been well-documented that autophagy not only is an autonomous mechanism that modulates cell homeostasis at basal level, but it is also involved in B-cell development and proliferation [11], cell survival [12,13], apoptosis [14,15], tumorigenesis, anti-tumoral immune responses [16], and resistance to chemotherapeutic agents. In this regard, a growing number of studies have suggested that autophagy shapes anti-tumoral immune responses by acting at multiple levels [17]. This includes the promotion of signals to activate phagocytosis of tumor cells [18,19], as well as signals to induce myeloid cell recruitment [20], MHC-class-I and -II presentation [21], B- and T-cell activation, development, maintenance [11,22], and self-tolerance [23]. Strikingly, experimental studies have demonstrated that the inhibition of autophagy enhances the sensitivity of MM cells to a number of anticancer agents and induces MM cell death [24,25]. Based on these findings, it has been suggested that autophagy could be targeted to treat MM [5,24,26] and recent studies and clinical trials have indeed confirmed the therapeutic implications of new and less toxic autophagy inhibitors in MM, used in combination with current anti-MM drugs [27,28,29].In support of a possible role of autophagy in MM, it was reported that aberrant expression of autophagy-related genes is associated with cancer development [30] and that multiple activators of autophagy or specific autophagy-related genes are commonly found in cancer-associated regions [31]. Interestingly, it was also described that expression of autophagy-related genes influences the response to conventional treatments in MM [32,33,34] and, thereby, disease progression [35,36], arguing that they may be useful to predict disease risk [37]. However, despite these findings suggesting a key role of autophagy in the etiology of MM and the existence of a genetic component controlling this catalytic process in MM, so far only ULK4, ATG5, and CDKN2A polymorphisms have been suggested to have an impact on the risk of MM [38,39]. Therefore, it is vital to perform a systematic analysis of autophagy-related markers to identify new susceptibility variants for MM and validate those associations already reported.In this context, the aim of this study was to comprehensively evaluate the impact of common genetic variation of 234 autophagy-related genes in determining the risk of developing MM. We also assessed the influence of the most promising markers on modulating immune responses in whole blood, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDM) from a large population of healthy donors from the Human Functional Genomic Project (HFGP). Additionally, we measured the autophagy flux in an independent population.2. Results2.1. abstracts.title: Gitelman syndrome: consensus and guidance from a Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Controversies Conference.
abstracts.abstract: Gitelman syndrome (GS) is a rare, salt-losing tubulopathy characterized by hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria. The disease is recessively inherited, caused by inactivating mutations in the SLC12A3 gene that encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC). GS is usually detected during adolescence or adulthood, either fortuitously or in association with mild or nonspecific symptoms or both. The disease is characterized by high phenotypic variability and a significant reduction in the quality of life, and it may be associated with severe manifestations. GS is usually managed by a liberal salt intake together with oral magnesium and potassium supplements. A general problem in rare diseases is the lack of high quality evidence to inform diagnosis, prognosis, and management. We report here on the current state of knowledge related to the diagnostic evaluation, follow-up, management, and treatment of GS; identify knowledge gaps; and propose a research agenda to substantiate a number of issues related to GS. This expert consensus statement aims to establish an initial framework to enable clinical auditing and thus improve quality control of care.

abstracts.title: Thiazide-sensitive Na+-Cl- cotransporter: genetic polymorphisms and human diseases.
abstracts.abstract: The thiazide-sensitive Na(+)-Cl(-) cotransporter (TSC) is responsible for the major sodium chloride reabsorption pathway, which is located in the apical membrane of the epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule. TSC is involved in several physiological activities including transepithelial ion absorption and secretion, cell volume regulation, and setting intracellular Cl(-) concentration below or above its electrochemical potential equilibrium. In addition, TSC serves as the target of thiazide-type diuretics that are the first line of therapy for the treatment of hypertension in the clinic, and its mutants are also reported to be associated with the hereditary disease, Gitelman's syndrome. This review aims to summarize the publications with regard to the TSC by focusing on the association between TSC mutants and human hypertension as well as Gitelman's syndrome.
